passage: The hostel common room smelled of instant coffee when Mehak put her phone face down on the table. Sonali looked up from her lab record. "Your papa again?" Mehak nodded. "I told him I'm taking the design elective next semester instead of the extra accounts paper. He said the firm has carried the family name for three generations and I'm being ungrateful. Then Mummy came on and said college has made me lost." She pressed her thumbs against her eyes. "Maybe I am. I don't even know if I hate accounts or just never chose them." Sonali pushed her own mug across the table. "So find out. Take the elective and see how it feels." Mehak drew two columns in the margin of her notebook, one headed Mine? and the other Handed to me. Both stayed half empty until lights-out.

qa.q: What did Mehak tell her papa she was taking next semester?
qa.a: She told him she was taking the design elective instead of the extra accounts paper.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she pressed her thumbs against her eyes?
qa.a: She felt guilty and hurt at being called ungrateful and lost, and also unsure, because she admits she doesn't know if she hates accounts or just never chose them.

qa.q: When Mehak drew the two columns, what choice was she making, and how could she use it?
qa.a: She chose to sort honestly what was hers from what was handed to her, instead of simply obeying or rebelling. Trying the elective would give her real answers for the Mine? column.

qa.q: How might Mehak's papa see the elective differently from Mehak?
qa.a: To him the firm carries three generations of family name, so a change can feel like turning away from the family; to Mehak it is a way to find out what she actually likes.

grounding: A young adult who questions the family career is called ungrateful and lost, and feels guilt while trying to sort what is truly hers from what was inherited.

passage:
Dear Sunaina didi,
You're the only one in the family I can write this to without the whole group chat finding out. I didn't sit for the prelims this year. I told Papa at Diwali, and Chacha said, loud enough for everyone, "Three generations of officers and this girl is lost." Papa didn't defend me. Later he said I was being ungrateful after all those coaching fees.
I keep replaying it at night here in my room in Pune. I do feel guilty. The fees were real. But I've started asking which parts of the plan were ever mine. Wanting to work with people and be useful, I think that's mine. The exact exam, the exact uniform, I'm not sure.
Is it wrong to take a year to find out? You left engineering once. Did anyone talk to you for a while after?
Love,
Nandini

qa.q: Where is Nandini while she writes this letter?
qa.a: She is in her room in Pune.

qa.q: Why does Nandini feel guilty even while she questions the plan?
qa.a: She knows the coaching fees were real, so stepping away feels like wasting what her family gave, even though she's not sure the exam path was ever hers.

qa.q: What choice is Nandini weighing when she asks about taking a year, and what could guide it?
qa.a: She is choosing between going back to the inherited exam path and taking time to test what she wants. Starting from the part she's sure of, working with people, could guide what she tries.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina understand Nandini better than the rest of the family?
qa.a: Sunaina once left engineering too, so she may know how it feels to be called lost and how lonely the silence afterwards can be.

grounding: A young adult who steps off the family's exam path is called lost and ungrateful, feels guilty and alone, and asks which parts of the plan were ever hers.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: You asked why I went quiet at the wedding, Kamal. Okay. My family has run the sweet shop in the old market for four generations, and everyone assumes I'll take the counter after Dadaji. At the wedding my Bua asked when I'm starting. I said I'm not sure I want to. Just that. And she said, "Such an ungrateful girl, Arohi. That shop fed you." After that my cousins kept forgetting to call me for photos. I laughed it off, but on the drive home I felt like the only person in the car. Here's what I can't explain to them. I love the shop. The smell of ghee at six in the morning, Dadaji's hands folding the boxes. I just don't know if I love it the way you love something you chose, or the way you love the wallpaper you grew up with. I want time to find out without being treated like a traitor.

qa.q: How long has Arohi's family run the sweet shop?
qa.a: For four generations, in the old market.

qa.q: What does Arohi feel unsure about when comparing the shop to the wallpaper she grew up with?
qa.a: She's unsure whether her love for the shop is truly her own choice or only familiarity, and not knowing leaves her confused and lonely.

qa.q: What choice does Arohi face after her Bua's comment, and what could help her?
qa.a: She can give in to avoid being seen as a traitor, or ask for time to test whether the shop is really hers. Talking it through with a friend like Kamal is a first honest step.

qa.q: How might Arohi's Bua see Arohi's hesitation?
qa.a: In her eyes the shop fed Arohi, so hesitating to take it over looks like ingratitude rather than an honest question.

grounding: A young adult who is unsure about taking over the family shop is called ungrateful, feels left out, and wants time to learn what is truly hers.

passage:
I'm Ramesh. I share a hostel room with Jatin, so I only know what I saw and heard. In August he told his father he wanted to try the journalism elective before deciding whether to stay in law, like his father and grandfather. The calls changed after that. His father's voice came out of the phone loud enough for me to hear "ungrateful" twice. His mother only said, "You've got lost, beta."
Jatin stopped going home at weekends. He'd sit on his bed with two lists, one headed mine and one headed theirs, moving things between them. Once he asked me, "Do I even like arguing, or did I just grow up at that dinner table?" I didn't know what to say. He ate dinner alone a lot that month. I wish I'd sat with him more.

qa.q: What were Jatin's two lists headed?
qa.a: One was headed mine and one was headed theirs.

qa.q: What does Jatin's question about arguing suggest he is trying to work out?
qa.a: He is trying to tell apart what he truly enjoys from what he simply absorbed growing up at his family's dinner table.

qa.q: When Jatin asked that question, what could Ramesh have done instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Ramesh could have sat with him and asked what he had noticed so far, so Jatin felt less alone while sorting it out.

qa.q: How might Jatin's father see the journalism elective, and why might that differ from Jatin's view?
qa.a: His father seems to hear it as ingratitude toward the family path, while for Jatin it is an honest question about what is really his.

grounding: A roommate describes a law student called ungrateful and lost for questioning the family career, who grows lonely while sorting what is his from what was handed down.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
Sunday. After lunch Elizabeth, twenty, told her mother she wanted to stop going to the morning service for a while, just to think about what she herself believes. Her mother set down the plates. "After everything this family gave you? Ungrateful. You've lost your way." Elizabeth said sorry and went to her room, though she wasn't sure what for.
Wednesday. In the college library she drew two columns: what I still hold, and what I'm not sure of yet. Kindness to strangers, grace before meals and her grandmother's hymns went in the first. She sat alone until closing, too guilty to phone home and too unsure to talk to anyone.
Two weeks later. Anjali found her on the hostel steps. "You've been vanishing." Elizabeth showed her the columns. Anjali read them slowly and didn't argue. It was the first evening in weeks that Elizabeth didn't feel alone with the question.

qa.q: What two columns did Elizabeth draw in the library?
qa.a: What I still hold, and what I'm not sure of yet.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth say sorry to her mother, though she wasn't sure what for?
qa.a: She felt guilty for hurting her mother, even though she didn't believe asking honest questions was wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Elizabeth's loneliness?
qa.a: Showing the columns to Anjali, who read them slowly without arguing, so she no longer carried the question alone.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth's mother be feeling when she calls her ungrateful?
qa.a: Her mother may feel hurt and afraid of losing something they share, even though it comes out as blame.

grounding: A young woman questioning her family's belief is called ungrateful and lost, feels guilt and loneliness, and tries to sort what she holds from what she inherited.
